Therefore, the union of neighbors is: \[\mathcal{N}(5) \cup \mathcal{N}(3) = \{1, 2, 4, 6\}\]

title: Graph Metrics
text:
Asymmetric Ties & Directed Graphs

Some relationships have an inherent directionality (asymmetric ties):

e.g., “A helps B”, “A seeks advice from B”.

Unlike symmetric ties, mutuality or reciprocity is not guaranteed by definition.
Reciprocity is an empirical event in the world (mutuality must be measured rather than assumed).

title: Graph Metrics
text:
Anti-Symmetric Ties & Hierarchies

Some directional relationships strictly forbid reciprocity (anti-symmetric ties):

If \(A \rightarrow B\) exists, then \(B \rightarrow A\) is structurally or logically impossible (\(AB \implies \neg BA\)).
e.g., “A is the father of B”, “A is the supervisor of B”.

Unlike asymmetric ties, reciprocity is not optional—it is strictly prohibited.
Concatenating these relations across multiple nodes naturally generates directed trees or strict hierarchies with no cycles.

title: Graph Metrics
text:
Directed Graph Representation

Asymmetric networks are represented as a directed graph (or digraph):

Simple lines are replaced with arrows indicating directionality.
Every edge has a source node (sender) and a destination node (receiver).
Unlike undirected graphs, node order matters: edge \(AB\) is distinct from \(BA\).

title: Graph Metrics
text:
Directed Graph: An Example



Let’s look at the digraph on the right:

Arrows indicate the direction of the relationship.
Some ties are reciprocated (e.g., \(A \leftrightarrow B\) and \(B \leftrightarrow D\)).
Others are strictly asymmetric (e.g., \(E \rightarrow C\), \(G \rightarrow F\)).

title: Graph Metrics
text:
Neighborhoods in Directed Graphs (1)



Because links are directional, nodes have two neighborhoods.
In-Neighborhood (\(N^{in}(v)\)):

Set of source nodes pointing to \(v\).
Example: \(N^{in}(D) = \{B, E, G\}\) (highlighted in gold, pointing to focal node D in tomato).

title: Graph Metrics
text:
Neighborhoods in Directed Graphs (2)



Out-Neighborhood (\(N^{out}(v)\)):

Set of destination nodes that \(v\) points to.
Example: \(N^{out}(B) = \{A, C, D\}\) (highlighted in gold, pointing from focal node B in tomato).

title: Graph Metrics
text:
Directed Neighborhoods: Reciprocity



A node appears in both neighborhoods only if there is a reciprocal (mutual) tie.
Example for Node B (in tomato):

In-Neighborhood: \(N^{in}(B) = \{A\}\)
Out-Neighborhood: \(N^{out}(B) = \{A, C, D\}\)

title: Graph Metrics
text:
Directed Neighborhoods: Reciprocity Overlap



Since there is a reciprocal tie \(A \leftrightarrow B\), node A (in gold) belongs to both sets.
Therefore, the overlap is the intersection of these two neighborhoods: \[N^{in}(B) \cap N^{out}(B) = \{A\}\]

title: Graph Metrics
text:
Directed Neighborhood Intersection

In directed graphs, neighborhood intersections can be defined for incoming or outgoing ties:
In-Neighborhood Intersection: Common source nodes pointing to both \(u\) and \(v\):

\(N^{in}(D) \cap N^{in}(A) = \{B\}\) (Node \(B\) points to both \(D\) and \(A\))

Out-Neighborhood Intersection: Common destination nodes that both \(u\) and \(v\) point to:

\(N^{out}(B) \cap N^{out}(E) = \{D\}\) (Both \(B\) and \(E\) point to \(D\))

title: Graph Metrics
text:
Directed Neighborhood Intersection: Example



Let’s visualize the out-neighborhood intersection of nodes B and E (in tomato):

\(N^{out}(B) = \{A, C, D\}\)
\(N^{out}(E) = \{D\}\)

They share one common destination node:

\(N^{out}(B) \cap N^{out}(E) = \{D\}\) (in gold)

title: Graph Metrics
text:
Directed Neighborhood Union

Similarly, directed neighborhood unions combine the sets of neighbors:
In-Neighborhood Union: Nodes pointing to either \(u\) or \(v\):

\(N^{in}(D) \cup N^{in}(A) = \{B, E, G\}\)

Out-Neighborhood Union: Nodes that either \(u\) or \(v\) points to:

\(N^{out}(B) \cup N^{out}(E) = \{A, C, D\}\)

title: Graph Metrics
text:
Directed Neighborhood Union: Example



Let’s visualize the out-neighborhood union of nodes B and E (in tomato):

\(N^{out}(B) = \{A, C, D\}\)
\(N^{out}(E) = \{D\}\)

Combining all unique destination nodes gives:

\(N^{out}(B) \cup N^{out}(E) = \{A, C, D\}\) (in gold)

title: Graph Metrics
text:
Symmetric Directed Graphs



Symmetric Directed Graph:

A digraph where for every directed arc \(u \rightarrow v\), the reverse arc \(v \rightarrow u\) is also present.
Formally: \(AB \iff BA\).

Key Properties:

It is a directed representation of an undirected (symmetric) graph.
Every connected dyad is reciprocal (Mutual).

title: Graph Metrics
text:
Functional Graphs



Functional Graph:

A directed graph where every node has an outdegree of exactly 1: \[k^{out}_v = 1 \quad \text{for all } v \in V\]

Key Properties:

Represents a single-valued function \(f: V \rightarrow V\), mapping each node to exactly one target.
e.g., “Who is your best friend?” or “Who is your immediate boss?”

title: Graph Metrics
text:
Oriented Graphs



Oriented Graph:

A directed graph obtained by choosing a single direction for each edge in an undirected graph.

Key Properties:

No reciprocal (mutual) arcs can exist: if \(u \rightarrow v\) is present, then \(v \rightarrow u\) is forbidden.
Represents purely non-reciprocal systems of interaction or asymmetric flows.

title: Graph Metrics
text:
Directed Tree Graphs



Directed Tree Graph:

A directed, acyclic graph where a single root node has an indegree of 0, and all other nodes have an indegree of exactly 1: \[k^{in}_{root} = 0 \quad \text{and} \quad k^{in}_v = 1 \quad \text{for all other } v\]

Key Properties:

Naturally models strict authority hierarchies or family trees.
Every node has exactly one parent or supervisor, with zero loops or overlapping chains of command.

title: Graph Metrics
text:
Node Degree in Undirected Graphs

In an undirected graph, a node’s degree (\(k_i\)) has two equivalent definitions:

Neighborhood Cardinality: The number of neighbors of node \(i\) (\(k_i = |\mathcal{N}(i)|\)).
Incident Edges Count: The number of edges connected to node \(i\).

Sociological meaning: Degree Centrality (reflects popularity, influence, or activity).

title: Graph Metrics
text:
Node Degree: An Example



Let’s calculate the degree for Node A (in tomato) on the right:

Neighbors of A: \(\mathcal{N}(A) = \{B, C, D, F\}\)
Neighborhood size: \(k_A = |\mathcal{N}(A)| = 4\)
Incident edges: \(AB\), \(AC\), \(AD\), and \(AF\) (\(k_A = 4\))

Thus, the degree of Node A is 4.

title: Graph Metrics
text:
Endpoints in Undirected Graphs

Endpoints (or leaves/periphery):

Nodes that have a degree equal to one (\(k_i = 1\)).
They have just a single neighbor in the graph.

title: Graph Metrics
text:
Endpoints: An Example



Let’s identify the endpoints in the graph on the right:

Nodes C and F (in tomato) are connected only to node A.
Since \(k_C = 1\) and \(k_F = 1\), they have degree one.
Therefore, C and F are the endpoints of this graph.

title: Graph Metrics
section: Node Degree in Directed Graphs: Indegree
text:
Node Degree in Directed Graphs: Indegree

Directed graphs have two distinct degrees for each node.
Indegree (\(k^{in}_i\)):

Number of edges pointing to node \(i\) (cardinality of \(N^{in}(i)\)).
Sociological meaning: Popularity, Prestige, or Status.

title: Graph Metrics
text:
Indegree: An Example



Let’s find the indegree for Node D (in tomato) on the right:

Source nodes pointing to D: \(N^{in}(D) = \{B, E, G\}\) (in gold)
Indegree: \(k^{in}_D = |N^{in}(D)| = 3\)

Node D has 3 incoming arrows, representing a node with relatively high popularity or status.

title: Graph Metrics
section: Node Degree in Directed Graphs: Outdegree
text:
Node Degree in Directed Graphs: Outdegree

Outdegree (\(k^{out}_i\)):

Number of edges pointing from node \(i\) (cardinality of \(N^{out}(i)\)).
Sociological meaning: Sociability or Activity.

title: Graph Metrics
text:
Outdegree: An Example



Let’s find the outdegree for Node B (in tomato) on the right:

Target nodes that B points to: \(N^{out}(B) = \{A, C, D\}\) (in gold)
Outdegree: \(k^{out}_B = |N^{out}(B)| = 3\)

Node B has 3 outgoing arrows, representing a node with relatively high sociability or activity.

title: Graph Metrics
section: Types of Nodes in Directed Graphs
text:
Types of Nodes in Directed Graphs

In a directed graph, we can distinguish three types of (non-isolate) nodes based on incoming and outgoing ties:

Receivers: Nodes that receive ties but do not send them (\(k_{in} > 0\) and \(k_{out} = 0\)).
Transmitters: Nodes that send ties but do not receive them (\(k_{in} = 0\) and \(k_{out} > 0\)).
Carriers: Nodes that both receive and send ties (\(k_{in} > 0\) and \(k_{out} > 0\)).

title: Graph Metrics
text:
Node Types: An Example



Looking at the directed graph on the right:

Receiver: Node C (only receives ties).
Transmitters: Nodes E and G (only send ties).
Carriers: Nodes A, B, D, F (both receive and send ties).

title: Graph Metrics
text:
Graph Order and Size

Graph Order (\(n\)):

The number of nodes in the graph (\(n = |V|\)).
Cardinality of the vertex set.

Graph Size (\(m\)):

The number of edges in the graph (\(m = |E|\)).
Cardinality of the edge set.

title: Graph Metrics
text:
Order and Size: Undirected Example



Let’s look at the undirected graph on the right:

Node Set (\(V\)): \(\{A, B, C, D, E, F, G\}\)
Edge Set (\(E\)): \(\{AC, CD, DG,\)  \(BE, EF, FB, CB\}\)
Graph Order (\(n = |V|\)): 7 nodes
Graph Size (\(m = |E|\)): 7 edges

title: Graph Metrics
text:
Order and Size: Directed Example



Let’s look at the directed graph on the right:

Node Set (\(V\)): \(\{A, B, C, D, E, G\}\)
Edge Set (\(E\)): \(\{BA, BC, BD, ED,\)  \(GD, AE, CG, AB\}\)
Graph Order (\(n = |V|\)): 6 nodes
Graph Size (\(m = |E|\)): 8 edges

title: Graph Metrics
text:
Graph Maximum Size

The maximum size of a simple graph of order \(n\) is the number of edges in a complete graph (where every node is connected to every other node).
Undirected: \(Max(E) = \frac{n(n - 1)}{2}\)
Directed: \(Max(E) = n(n - 1)\)

title: Graph Metrics
text:
Maximum Size: Undirected Example



Let’s look at the undirected graph on the right:

Order (\(n\)): 7 nodes

Formula: \[Max(E) = \frac{n(n - 1)}{2}\]

title: Graph Metrics
text:
Maximum Size: Undirected Calculation



Order (\(n\)): 7 nodes (shown on the right)
Maximum possible size calculation: \[Max(E) = \frac{7 \times (7 - 1)}{2} = \frac{42}{2} = 21\text{ edges}\]
Interpretation:

A complete undirected graph with 7 nodes would have exactly 21 edges.

title: Graph Metrics
text:
Maximum Size: Directed Example



Let’s look at the directed graph on the right:

Order (\(n\)): 6 nodes

Formula: \[Max(E) = n(n - 1)\]

title: Graph Metrics
text:
Maximum Size: Directed Calculation



Order (\(n\)): 6 nodes (shown on the right)
Maximum possible size calculation: \[Max(E) = 6 \times (6 - 1) = 6 \times 5 = 30\text{ edges}\]
Interpretation:

A complete directed graph with 6 nodes would have exactly 30 directed arcs.

title: Graph Metrics
text:
Graph Density: Formulas

Density (\(d\)) is the ratio of the observed number of edges (\(m\)) to the maximum possible number of edges.
It is a value between 0 (completely empty) and 1 (complete graph).
Undirected Graph: \[d = \frac{2m}{n(n-1)}\]

title: Graph Metrics
text:
Graph Density: Formulas

Density (\(d\)) is the ratio of the observed number of edges (\(m\)) to the maximum possible number of edges.
It is a value between 0 (completely empty) and 1 (complete graph).
Directed Graph: \[d = \frac{m}{n(n-1)}\]

title: Graph Metrics
text:
Graph Density: Interpretation

Connection Probability:

Density is the probability that any two randomly chosen nodes are connected.

Network Resilience:

Denser networks are generally more resilient and less vulnerable to breakdowns when key nodes are removed.

title: Graph Metrics
text:
Density: Undirected Example



Let’s look at the undirected graph on the right:

Order (\(n\)): 7 nodes
Size (\(m\)): 7 edges
Maximum possible edges: \[Max(E) = \frac{7 \times 6}{2} = 21\]

title: Graph Metrics
text:
Density: Undirected Calculation



Observed edges (\(m\)): 7 (shown on the right)
Maximum possible edges: 21
Density Formula: \[d = \frac{m}{Max(E)} = \frac{7}{21} \approx 0.333\]
Interpretation:

Exactly 33.3% of all possible undirected ties are present in this network.

title: Graph Metrics
text:
Density: Directed Example



Let’s look at the directed graph on the right:

Order (\(n\)): 6 nodes
Size (\(m\)): 8 directed edges
Maximum possible edges: \[Max(E) = 6 \times 5 = 30\]

title: Graph Metrics
text:
Density: Directed Calculation



Observed directed edges (\(m\)): 8 (shown on the right)
Maximum possible edges: 30
Density Formula: \[d = \frac{m}{Max(E)} = \frac{8}{30} \approx 0.267\]
Interpretation:

Exactly 26.7% of all possible directed ties are present in this network.

title: Graph Metrics
text:
Graph Degree Set and Sequence



Graph Degree Set: A list of the degrees of every node in the graph.
Graph Degree Sequence: The degree set sorted in descending order.
This provides a “fingerprint” of the graph’s overall connectivity structure.

title: Graph Metrics
text:
Degree Set & Sequence: Undirected Example



Degrees: \(k_A=1, k_B=3, k_C=3, k_D=2, k_E=2, k_F=2, k_G=1\) (shown on the right)
Degree Set (unordered list of node degrees): \[\{1, 3, 3, 2, 2, 2, 1\}\]
Degree Sequence (sorted degrees): \[(3, 3, 2, 2, 2, 1, 1)\]

title: Graph Metrics
text:
In-Degree Set & Sequence: Directed Example



In-Degrees: \(k^{in}_A=1, k^{in}_B=1, k^{in}_C=1, k^{in}_D=3, k^{in}_E=1, k^{in}_G=1\) (shown on the right)
In-Degree Set (unordered list of in-degrees): \[\{1, 1, 1, 3, 1, 1\}\]
In-Degree Sequence (sorted in-degrees): \[(3, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1)\]

title: Graph Metrics
text:
Out-Degree Set & Sequence: Directed Example



Out-Degrees: \(k^{out}_A=2, k^{out}_B=3, k^{out}_C=1, k^{out}_D=0, k^{out}_E=1, k^{out}_G=1\) (shown on the right)
Out-Degree Set (unordered list of out-degrees): \[\{2, 3, 1, 0, 1, 1\}\]
Out-Degree Sequence (sorted out-degrees): \[(3, 2, 1, 1, 1, 0)\]

title: Graph Metrics
text:
Degree Range & Sum



Maximum Degree (\(k_{max}\)) and Minimum Degree (\(k_{min}\)).
Degree Range (\(k_r\)): \(k_{max} - k_{min}\).
Sum of Degrees (\(\sum k_i\)):

In an undirected graph, this is always twice the number of edges: \(\sum k_i = 2m\).

title: Graph Metrics
text:
Degree Range & Sum: Example



Degrees: \(k_A=1, k_B=3, k_C=3, k_D=2, k_E=2, k_F=2, k_G=1\) (shown on the right)
Max & Min Degree:

\(k_{max} = 3\) (nodes B and C)
\(k_{min} = 1\) (nodes A and G)

Degree Range:

\(k_r = 3 - 1 = 2\)

Sum of Degrees:

\(\sum k_i = 1+3+3+2+2+2+1 = 14 = 2m\) (Matches!)

title: Graph Metrics
text:
Graphical vs. Non-Graphical Sequences

A sequence of non-negative integers is graphical if there exists at least one simple, undirected graph (no loops, no multiple edges) that has it as its degree sequence.
Otherwise, the sequence is non-graphical—no such simple graph can possibly exist in the real world.
Why can’t certain sequences exist?

They violate core mathematical rules of graph structure!

title: Graph Metrics
text:
Two Quick Tests for Graphicality
Before using complex algorithms, we can apply two fast screening tests:

The Even Sum Rule (Handshake Lemma):

The sum of degrees must be even: \(\sum k_i = 2m\).
If the sum of a sequence is odd, it is automatically non-graphical!

The Maximum Degree Bound:

In a simple graph of order \(n\), no node can have a degree larger than \(n-1\).
If any degree in the sequence exceeds \(n-1\), it is automatically non-graphical!

title: Graph Metrics
text:
Graphicality: Concrete Examples

Graphical Sequence: \(\mathbf{d} = (4, 3, 3, 2, 2, 1, 1)\) with \(n = 7\)

Sum is \(16\) (even). Max degree is \(4 \le 6\).
A real simple graph can easily be constructed with these degrees.

Non-Graphical Sequence (Odd Sum Violation): \(\mathbf{d} = (4, 3, 3, 3, 2, 1, 1)\) with \(n = 7\)

Sum is \(17\) (odd). Violates Handshake Lemma.
No simple graph can ever have this sequence.

Non-Graphical Sequence (Degree Bound Violation): \(\mathbf{d} = (7, 2, 2, 1)\) with \(n = 4\)

Max degree is \(7\), which is greater than \(n-1 = 3\).
A node in a 4-person group cannot have 7 unique friends!

title: Graph Metrics
text:
Average Degree



Average Degree (\(\bar{k}\)): The average of all node degrees in the graph.
\[\bar{k} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} k_i = \frac{2m}{n}\]
It represents the expected degree of a randomly chosen node.
It is also directly related to density, which we will derive on the next slides!

title: Graph Metrics
text:
Connecting Density & Average Degree

There is an intimate mathematical relationship between density (\(d\)) and average degree (\(\bar{k}\)).
Recall the undirected density formula: \[d = \frac{2m}{n(n-1)}\]
We can rewrite this by pulling out the average degree term (\(\bar{k} = \frac{2m}{n}\)): \[d = \left(\frac{2m}{n}\right) \times \frac{1}{n-1} = \bar{k} \times \frac{1}{n-1} = \frac{\bar{k}}{n-1} \qquad \iff \qquad \bar{k} = d(n-1)\]

title: Graph Metrics
text:
Interpreting the Density-Degree Connection

Density is Average Degree Scaled by Group Size:

The density of an undirected graph is simply its average degree divided by the maximum possible connections of any single node (\(n-1\)).

For Example:

In a group of \(n = 10\) people, each person can have at most \(n-1 = 9\) connections.
If the average number of friends (\(\bar{k}\)) is \(4.5\), then the density of friendship is: \[d = \frac{4.5}{9} = 0.50 \quad (50\%)\]

Directed Case:

The exact same identity holds! Since \(d^d = \frac{m}{n(n-1)}\) and {k} is \(\frac{m}{n}\), we get: \[d^d = \frac{\bar{k}}{n-1}\]

title: Graph Metrics
text:
Degree Variance



Degree Variance (\(\sigma^2_k\)): A measure of how much the node degrees vary from the average degree.
\[\sigma^2_k = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} (k_i - \bar{k})^2\]
A low variance mean less inequality in connectivity (more homogeneous), while a high variance indicates more inequality (more heterogeneous).

title: Graph Metrics
text:
Degree Metrics: Basic Example



Node Degrees: \(k_A=1, k_B=3, k_C=3, k_D=2, k_E=2, k_F=2, k_G=1\) (shown on the right)
Degree Set: \(\{1, 3, 3, 2, 2, 2, 1\}\) (degrees of all nodes in the graph)
Degree Sequence: \((3, 3, 2, 2, 2, 1, 1)\) (ordered from highest to lowest)
Degree Sum: \[\sum k_i = 1+3+3+2+2+2+1 = 14 = 2m\]

title: Graph Metrics
text:
Degree Metrics: Average Degree



Degrees: \(k_A=1, k_B=3, k_C=3, k_D=2, k_E=2, k_F=2, k_G=1\) (shown on the right)
Order (\(n\)): 7 nodes
Average Degree (\(\bar{k}\)): \[\bar{k} = \frac{\sum k_i}{n} = \frac{14}{7} = 2.0\]

title: Graph Metrics
text:
Degree Metrics: Degree Variance



Degrees: \(k_A=1, k_B=3, k_C=3, k_D=2, k_E=2, k_F=2, k_G=1\) (shown on the right)
Degree Variance (\(\sigma^2_k\)): \[\sigma^2_k = \frac{\sum (k_i - \bar{k})^2}{n}\]
Variance Calculation: \[\sigma^2_k = \frac{3 \times (2-2)^2 + 2 \times (3-2)^2 + 2 \times (1-2)^2}{7} = \frac{4}{7} \approx 0.571\]

title: Graph Metrics
text:
Regular Graphs



A regular graph is one where every node has the same degree \(k\) (called \(k\)-regular).
Since all node degrees are identical to the average, the degree variance is zero (\(\sigma^2_k = 0\)).
These are rare in real-world social networks but are used as baseline models.
Example: A 3-regular graph on 6 nodes (shown on the right).

title: Graph Metrics
text:
Regular Graphs: Metrics Example



Node Degrees: \(k_A=3, k_B=3, k_C=3, k_D=3, k_E=3, k_F=3\) (shown on the right)
Order (\(n\)): 6 nodes
Average Degree (\(\bar{k}\)): \[\bar{k} = \frac{\sum k_i}{n} = \frac{18}{6} = 3.0\]

title: Graph Metrics
text:
Regular Graphs: Variance Example



Average Degree (\(\bar{k}\)): 3.0 (shown on the right)
Degree Variance (\(\sigma^2_k\)): \[\sigma^2_k = \frac{6 \times (3 - 3)^2}{6} = 0\]
Conclusion:

Since every node’s degree matches the average degree, the deviation is zero for all nodes, resulting in zero variance.

title: Graph Metrics
text:
Average Nearest Neighbor Degree



Average Nearest Neighbor Degree (\(\bar{k}_{nn(i)}\)) measures the average degree of node \(i\)’s neighbors.
Formula: \[\bar{k}_{nn(i)} = \frac{1}{k_i} \sum_{j \in \mathcal{N}(i)} k_j\]
It tells us whether a node’s connections are, on average, highly connected or peripheral.

title: Graph Metrics
text:
Feld’s Friendship Paradox

Feld’s Friendship Paradox (Scott Feld, 1991):

In almost all social networks, the average degree of a node’s neighbors (\(\bar{k}_{nn}\)) is greater than the average degree of the nodes in the network (\(\bar{k}\)).

Why does this happen?

Highly connected individuals (popular hubs) belong to many people’s neighborhood sets, disproportionately inflating neighbor degrees across the network.

Your friends, on average, have more friends than you do!

title: Graph Metrics
text:
Friendship Paradox: Node Calculations (A-D)

For the undirected graph shown previously (average degree \(\bar{k} = 2.0\)):

Node A (neighbor C): \(\bar{k}_{nn(A)} = \frac{k_C}{1} = \frac{3}{1} = 3.0\)
Node B (neighbors C, E, F): \(\bar{k}_{nn(B)} = \frac{k_C + k_E + k_F}{3} = \frac{3 + 2 + 2}{3} \approx 2.33\)
Node C (neighbors A, D, B): \(\bar{k}_{nn(C)} = \frac{k_A + k_D + k_B}{3} = \frac{1 + 2 + 3}{3} = 2.0\)
Node D (neighbors C, G): \(\bar{k}_{nn(D)} = \frac{k_C + k_G}{2} = \frac{3 + 1}{2} = 2.0\)

title: Graph Metrics
text:
Friendship Paradox: Node Calculations (E-G)

Continuing calculations for the remaining nodes:

Node E (neighbors B, F): \(\bar{k}_{nn(E)} = \frac{k_B + k_F}{2} = \frac{3 + 2}{2} = 2.5\)
Node F (neighbors E, B): \(\bar{k}_{nn(F)} = \frac{k_E + k_B}{2} = \frac{2 + 3}{2} = 2.5\)
Node G (neighbor D): \(\bar{k}_{nn(G)} = \frac{k_D}{1} = \frac{2}{1} = 2.0\)

Summary of average neighbor degrees:

\(\bar{k}_{nn} = (3.0, 2.33, 2.0, 2.0, 2.5, 2.5, 2.0)\)

title: Graph Metrics
text:
Friendship Paradox: Network Average

From the node calculations on the previous slide, the average nearest neighbor degrees are:

\(\bar{k}_{nn} = (3.0, 2.33, 2.0, 2.0, 2.5, 2.5, 2.0)\)

Average neighbor degree for the network: \[\text{Mean}(\bar{k}_{nn}) = \frac{3.0 + 2.33 + 2.0 + 2.0 + 2.5 + 2.5 + 2.0}{7} \approx 2.33\]
Demonstrating the Paradox:

Average degree of nodes’ neighbors (\(\approx 2.33\)) is greater than the average degree of nodes (\(\bar{k} = 2.0\)).

title: Graph Metrics
text:
Directed Degree Sets & Sequences

Directed graphs have two distinct degree sets (In-Degree set and Out-Degree set) and two distinct sequences.
In our 6-node directed graph:

In-Degree Set: \(\{1, 1, 1, 3, 1, 1\}\)
In-Degree Sequence: \((3, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1)\)
Out-Degree Set: \(\{2, 3, 1, 0, 1, 1\}\)
Out-Degree Sequence: \((3, 2, 1, 1, 1, 0)\)

title: Graph Metrics
text:
Directed Degree Range & Sum

Like undirected graphs, we can define the maximum, minimum, and range of degrees.
In directed graphs, these are defined separately for in-degree and out-degree:

In-Degree Range: \(k^{in}_{max} - k^{in}_{min}\)
Out-Degree Range: \(k^{out}_{max} - k^{out}_{min}\)

Degree Sum Rule:

The sum of in-degrees and the sum of out-degrees are both equal to the graph size \(m\) (total number of directed edges/arcs): \(\sum_{i=1}^{n} k^{in}_i = \sum_{i=1}^{n} k^{out}_i = m\)

title: Graph Metrics
text:
Directed Range & Sum: Example



For our 6-node directed graph (shown again on the right, \(m = 8\)):

In-Degrees: \(k^{in} = (1, 1, 1, 3, 1, 1)\)

\(k^{in}_{max} = 3\) (Node D), \(k^{in}_{min} = 1\)
Range \(k^{in}_r = 3 - 1 = 2\)
Sum \(\sum k^{in}_i = 1+1+1+3+1+1 = 8\)

title: Graph Metrics
text:
Directed Range & Sum: Example



For our 6-node directed graph (shown again on the right, \(m = 8\)):

Out-Degrees: \(k^{out} = (2, 3, 1, 0, 1, 1)\)

\(k^{out}_{max} = 3\) (Node B), \(k^{out}_{min} = 0\) (Node D)
Range \(k^{out}_r = 3 - 0 = 3\)
Sum \(\sum k^{out}_i = 2+3+1+0+1+1 = 8\)

title: Graph Metrics
text:
Directed Average Degree

Average In-Degree (\(\bar{k}^{in}\)) and Average Out-Degree (\(\bar{k}^{out}\)): \(\bar{k}^{in} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} k^{in}_i \quad \text{and} \quad \bar{k}^{out} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} k^{out}_i\)
The Equivalence Theorem:

In every directed graph, the average in-degree is exactly equal to the average out-degree: \(\bar{k}^{in} = \bar{k}^{out} = \frac{m}{n}\)
Why? Each directed edge \(u \rightarrow v\) adds exactly 1 to the out-degree of \(u\) and exactly 1 to the in-degree of \(v\).

title: Graph Metrics
text:
Equivalence of Means: Example



In our 6-node directed graph:

Order (\(n\)): 6 nodes
Size (\(m\)): 8 directed edges

Mean In-Degree: \(\bar{k}^{in} = \frac{1+1+1+3+1+1}{6} = \frac{8}{6} \approx 1.33\)
Mean Out-Degree: \(\bar{k}^{out} = \frac{2+3+1+0+1+1}{6} = \frac{8}{6} \approx 1.33\)
They are equal! (\(\bar{k}^{in} = \bar{k}^{out} = 1.33 = m/n\))

title: Graph Metrics
text:
Directed Degree Variance

While the means are always equal, the variances of in-degree and out-degree can be completely different!
In-Degree Variance (\(\sigma^2_{in}\)): \(\sigma^2_{in} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} (k^{in}_i - \bar{k}^{in})^2\)

Sociological meaning: Measures inequality in prestige/popularity (do a few nodes receive all ties?).

Out-Degree Variance (\(\sigma^2_{out}\)): \(\sigma^2_{out} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} (k^{out}_i - \bar{k}^{out})^2\)

Sociological meaning: Measures inequality in sociability/activity (do some nodes send way more ties than others?).

text:
Directed Degree Variance: Example



In our 6-node directed graph:

Mean degree (\(\bar{k}\)) is \(\approx 1.33\)

In-Degree Variance (\(\sigma^2_{in}\)):

Values:

Calculation:

\(\frac{5 \times (1-1.33)^2 + 1 \times (3-1.33)^2}{6} =\)
\(\frac{5 \times 0.11 + 2.78}{6} \approx 0.556\)

title: Graph Metrics
text:
Directed Degree Variance: Example



In our 6-node directed graph:

Mean degree (\(\bar{k}\)) is \(\approx 1.33\)

Out-Degree Variance (\(\sigma^2_{out}\)):

Values:

\(k^{out} = (2, 3, 1, 0, 1, 1)\)

Calculation:

\(\frac{(2-1.33)^2 + (3-1.33)^2 + 3(1-1.33)^2 + (0-1.33)^2}{6} \approx 0.889\)


Out-degree is more heterogeneous than in-degree in this network!

title: Graph Metrics
text:
Comparing Density: Undirected vs. Directed

Maximum Possible Edges:

Undirected: \(Max(E)_{undir} = \frac{n(n - 1)}{2}\)
Directed: \(Max(E)_{dir} = n(n - 1)\)

Density Scaling:

Because a directed graph can hold exactly twice as many edges as an undirected graph of the same order: \(d_{dir} = \frac{1}{2} d_{undir} \quad \text{for the same } m \text{ and } n\)
Directed density is always more “conservative”—it requires twice as many edges as an undirected graph to reach the same level of density!

title: Measuring Ego Networks
section: Key Ego Network Metrics: Size and Homogeneity
text:
Key Ego Network Metrics: Size and Homogeneity
To analyze personal networks empirically, researchers compute specific structural properties based on ego-alter attributes and alter-alter connections.

1. Ego Network Size (\(S(Ego)\)):

The simplest metric: a count of the ego-to-alter ties (\(E_{ea}\)), equivalent to the degree (\(k^{Ego}\)) of the ego node.
\[S(Ego) = |N(Ego)| = |E_{ea}|\]

2. E-I Homophily Index (Krackhardt & Stern, 1988):

Measures in-group and out-group preference based on categorical attributes of ego and alters.
\[EI = \frac{External - Internal}{External + Internal}\]
Internal Ties (Int): Ties to alters who share the exact same category as Ego.
External Ties (Ext): Ties to alters in categories different from Ego.
Range: \([-1.0, +1.0]\)

-1.0: Complete Homophily (exclusively similar alters).
+1.0: Complete Heterophily (exclusively dissimilar alters).
0.0: Perfect Balance (equal number of internal and external ties).

title: Measuring Ego Networks
text:
Step-by-Step Metrics Calculation Example



Let’s trace the calculation for the network on the right:

Ego: Man (Blue)
Alters: 3 Men (Blue), 2 Women (Orange), 1 Nonbinary (Green).

1. Size (\(S\)):

\(S = 6\) alters.

2. E-I Homophily Index (Gender):

Internal (\(Int\)) = 3 (Alters 1, 2, 3 are Men, same as Ego)
External (\(Ext\)) = 3 (Alters 4, 5 are Women; Alter 6 is Nonbinary)
\[EI = \frac{3 - 3}{3 + 3} = \frac{0}{6} = 0.00\]
The network is in perfect balance, showing no structural bias toward ingroup or outgroup.

title: Measuring Ego Networks
section: Key Ego Network Metrics: Diversity and Clustering
text:
Key Ego Network Metrics: Diversity and Clustering

3. Blau’s Heterogeneity Index (\(H\)):

Measures overall sociodemographic diversity among alters. Crucially, Ego’s own attribute does not matter.
\[H = 1 - \sum_{k} p_k^2\]
Where \(p_k\) is the proportion of alters belonging to category \(k\).
Range: \([0.0, H_{max}]\)

0.0: No diversity (all alters belong to a single category).
Maximum Diversity (\(H_{max}\)): Occurs when categories are equally represented.
\[H_{max} = 1 - \frac{1}{k} \quad (\text{where } k \text{ is the number of available categories})\]


4. Clustering Coefficient (\(CC_i\)):

Measures the density of connections among alters, ignoring the ego and ego-to-alter edges.
\[CC_i = \frac{2m}{n(n-1)}\]
Where \(n\) is ego network size, and \(m\) is the count of alter-to-alter ties.
Range: \([0.0, 1.0]\). A \(CC = 0.20\) means 20% of all possible friendships among alters actually exist.

title: Measuring Ego Networks
text:
Summary of Measuring Ego Networks

Four Core Properties:

Size: How many alters in the network?
Homogeneity (E-I): How similar are alters to ego?
Diversity (H): How varied are the attributes of the alters?
Clustering (CC): To what extent do alters know one another?

Key Takeaways:

Choosing the right metric depends entirely on your research question.
Homogeneity and diversity are distinct: an ego network can have high homogeneity but low diversity, or vice versa, depending on group definitions.
Ego clustering measures network density, showing whether an ego is embedded in a single tight-knit circle or bridges separate, unconstrained social worlds.

title: Dunbar’s Theory of Social Circles
section: Levels of Analysis in Social Networks
text:
Levels of Analysis in Social Networks

As we move through social network analysis, we follow a natural progression:

Individual / Ego (the actor)
Dyads (pairs of actors and their tie properties)
Triads (triplets of actors and local structures)
Subgroups / Cliques / Communities (meso-level structures)
Whole Network (macro-level structures)

Ego Networks represent the personal network centered on a single actor (ego) and their connections (alters).

title: Dunbar’s Theory of Social Circles
section: Why Is the Human Brain So Big?
text:
Why Is the Human Brain So Big?

The Social Brain Hypothesis (Robin Dunbar, 2003)

In comparison to our closest primate ancestors, humans have exceptionally large brains (specifically the neocortex) relative to body size.
Why? Because humans are incredibly social animals!
Finding: Neocortex size scales with average social group size across primate species.
Explanation: The brain evolved primarily to manage complex social relationships—keeping track of who is who, who is allied with whom, and who is an enemy.

Dunbar’s Number (~150)

Extrapolating the primate curve to humans predicts a cognitive limit of about 150 stable relationships that an individual can maintain.

title: Dunbar’s Theory of Social Circles
text:
Visualizing the Social Brain Hypothesis



Empirical Evidence (Dunbar 1992, 2003)

Plotted across various primate species: prosimians, New World monkeys, Old World monkeys, and apes.
Neocortex Ratio (volume of neocortex divided by rest of brain) is strongly associated with average social group size.
The non-human primate regression line (solid line, \(R^2 = 0.84\)) represents a tight cognitive constraint.
Extrapolating to Humans:

A human neocortex ratio of ~4.1 predicts an average group size of ~150 (Dunbar’s number).

title: Dunbar’s Theory of Social Circles
section: The Concept of Ego Network Layers
text:
The Concept of Ego Network Layers

Ego networks are organized into concentric layers based on intimacy and closeness.
Closer layers are smaller and more intimate; farther layers are larger and less intimate.
Relationship Maintenance Costs:

Maintaining social ties is not free. Every tie requires investments of:

Cognitive/Emotional energy (empathy, mental tracking)
Time/Physical energy (interaction frequency, communication)

These maintenance costs naturally limit the number of people who can fit into each successive circle.

title: Dunbar’s Theory of Social Circles
section: Visualizing the Dunbar Circles: The Ego
text:
Visualizing the Dunbar Circles: The Ego



Your personal network expands outwards from you (Ego).
Let’s trace how these circles of intimacy build up, layer by layer, centered around the central actor…
Maintenance costs are zero when there are no ties to track!

title: Dunbar’s Theory of Social Circles
section: Visualizing the Dunbar Circles: Support Clique
text:
Visualizing the Dunbar Circles: Support Clique



Support Clique (~4–5 people)

Your most intimate kin and best friends.
High emotional and cognitive investment.
These are the people you can rely on in times of crisis and emergency (e.g., “the 3 AM call” if your car breaks down or you are hospitalized).

title: Dunbar’s Theory of Social Circles
section: Visualizing the Dunbar Circles: Sympathy Group
text:
Visualizing the Dunbar Circles: Sympathy Group



Sympathy Group (~12–15 people)

Close kin and good friends whom you interact with frequently.
Less intimate than the support clique but still highly valued.
These are the people with whom you share a strong bond and who provide mutual aid and services (e.g., helping you pack up and move to a new house).

title: Dunbar’s Theory of Social Circles
section: Visualizing the Dunbar Circles: Affinity Group
text:
Visualizing the Dunbar Circles: Affinity Group



Affinity Group (~45–50 people)

More casual but still close friends, extended family.
Frequent enough contact that you consider them part of your active social circle.
These are people you would invite to a birthday party or dinner, but whom you wouldn’t necessarily call in a crisis.

title: Dunbar’s Theory of Social Circles
section: Visualizing the Dunbar Circles: Active Network
text:
Visualizing the Dunbar Circles: Active Network



Active Network (~120–150 people)

The outermost boundary of meaningful personal relationships.
People you recognize by face and name (without digital aids) and interact with at least once a year.
These are people you consider when making decisions, or potential contacts for job opportunities.

title: Dunbar’s Theory of Social Circles
text:
Tie Strength & Dunbar Circles

We can map Granovetter’s Tie Strength (1973) directly onto Dunbar circles:

Strong Ties occupy the inner layers (Support Clique and Sympathy Group).
Weak Ties occupy the outer layers (Affinity Group and Active Network).

The Tradeoff of Network Structure:

Inner Circles (Strong Ties):

High trust, emotional intensity, and mutual aid.
Governed by g-transitivity (triadic closure): your close friends are likely friends with each other, leading to high density but highly redundant information.

Outer Circles (Weak Ties):

Violate transitivity (your acquaintances are rarely friends with each other).
Function as bridges connecting you to distant parts of the social structure, providing novel, diverse information.

title: Dunbar’s Theory of Social Circles
section: Dunbar Circles in the Digital Age
text:
Dunbar Circles in the Digital Age

Do social media websites (Facebook, Instagram, LinkedIn) break Dunbar’s limit?

Digital platforms allow us to have thousands of online “friends” and “connections.”
But can we maintain them?
Research Finding: No. Even on digital platforms, cognitive and emotional constraints remain.
While we can accumulate thousands of weak or passive ties, our active network size (those we actually interact with) and our intimate support clique sizes remain remarkably consistent with Dunbar’s predictions (~150 active contacts, ~4-5 close confidants).
Technology changes the ease of tracking weak ties, but it does not change the core limits of the human neocortex.

title: Dunbar’s Theory of Social Circles
text:
Summary of Key Takeaways

Ego Networks are Layered: Intimacy and group size are in an inverse relationship. Closer layers are smaller and require higher maintenance costs.
The Social Brain: Our cognitive and emotional capacity is the primary constraint on our social network size.
Functional Dualism:

The inner circles (strong ties) provide emotional support, trust, and safety.
The outer circles (weak ties) provide novelty, information, and bridges to other social networks.

title: Graph Theory: Blockmodeling
text:
The Correlation Distance (\(d^{corr}_{k,l}\))

Beyond Euclidean distance, we can measure structural similarity using the Pearson Correlation Coefficient (\(r_{kl}\) or \(d^{corr}_{kl}\)) between node vectors.
Compares row (or column) vectors and returns a value between \(-1.0\) and \(+1.0\):

\(+1.0\): Nodes are perfectly structurally equivalent.
Positive (\(> 0.0\)): Nodes are structurally similar.
Negative (\(< 0.0\)): Nodes are structurally dissimilar.
\(-1.0\): Nodes are completely different, pointing to completely disjoint sets of neighbors.

The formula is:

\[d^{corr}_{k, l} = \frac{\sum_j (a_{(k)j} - \overline{a}_{(k)j}) \times (a_{(l)j} - \overline{a}_{(l)j})}{\sqrt{\sum_j (a_{(k)j} - \overline{a}_{(k)j})^2 \times \sum_j (a_{(l)j} - \overline{a}_{(l)j})^2}}\]

title: Graph Theory: Blockmodeling
text:
Meaning of Row Means (\(\overline{a}_{(k)j}\))

What does \(\overline{a}_{(k)j}\) represent?

It is simply the average of the row elements for node \(k\).
\[\overline{a}_{(k)j} = \frac{\sum_j a_{kj}}{N}\]
Where \(N\) is the number of columns (the order of the graph).

For a binary adjacency matrix, the row mean is simply the node degree divided by the number of nodes:

Node \(A\) has ties to \(\{C, D\}\) in a 6-node network:
Vector \(a_{(A)j} = (0, 0, 1, 1, 0, 0)\).
Average: \(\overline{a}_{(A)j} = \frac{2}{6} \approx 0.33\).

Iterated Correlation Distances: CONCOR

What happens if we take the correlation distance of a correlation distance matrix?
CONCOR (Convergence of Iterated Correlations; Breiger, Boorman, & Arabie, 1975):

If we recursively calculate the correlation distance matrix of the previous correlation matrix, the values mathematically converge to only \(+1.0\) and \(-1.0\).
This slices the network into two distinct, highly clear-cut blocks of structurally equivalent or similar nodes.

title: Graph Theory: Blockmodeling
section: Uncovering Secret Patterns in Large Networks
text:
Uncovering Secret Patterns in Large Networks



Let’s apply CONCOR to a larger, messier 22-node network on the right.
It contains:

Three high-degree hub nodes (\(A\), \(B\), \(C\)).
Sets of identical peripheral leaf nodes connected to each hub.
A highly central node \(D\) bridging hubs.
Two peripheral nodes \(U, V\) connected only to \(S\).

Let’s see how CONCOR recursively partitions this graph.

title: Graph Theory: Blockmodeling
text:
Step 1: First Split (Two Giant Blocks)

Running CONCOR on the whole 22-node network splits it into two massive blocks:

Block 1: \(\{V, U, S, H, G, F, E, T, C, A, B\}\) (Colored Red)
Block 2: \(\{R, Q, P, O, N, M, L, K, J, D, I\}\) (Colored Blue)

title: Graph Theory: Blockmodeling
text:
Step 2: Going Deeper (The Hierarchical Partition)

Running CONCOR recursively on the induced subgraphs of each block yields nested subdivisions:

Block 1 Splits:

Block 1a (Core hub/bridge): \(\{A, B, C, S, U, V\}\)
Block 1b (A’s peripheral leaves): \(\{E, F, G, H, T\}\)

Block 2 Splits:

Block 2a (B’s peripheral leaves): \(\{I, J, K, L, M\}\)
Block 2b (C’s peripheral leaves): \(\{N, O, P, Q, R\}\)
Block 2c (Unique central bridge): \(\{D\}\) (Occupies a block entirely by itself!)


Further splits on Block 1a isolate \(\{U, V\}\), and divide the remaining \(\{A, B, C, S\}\) into \(\{A, S\}\) and \(\{B, C\}\).

text:
Final Seven-Block Partition

The final, elegant block partition reveals how role structures are naturally isolated:

We record a 1 if the relation block is a One Block (contains ties).

This yields a highly simplified map of role interactions:

text:
Blockmodeling: A Structural Summary

Blockmodeling Distills Structure:

Slices complex social structures down to high-level system blueprints.

CONCOR algorithm:

Recursively polarizes Pearson correlations to group similar actors.

Zero vs. One Blocks:

Blocked adjacency matrices cleanly isolate patterns of connection (One blocks) and absolute separation (Zero blocks).

Reduced Graph Models:

Image matrices represent relations between roles, creating simplified reduced graphs that make networks easy to read, interpret, and model.

title: What is A Social Network?
text:
What are social networks? As you saw in the tree chart shown in ?@fig-network-types in the previous lesson, only a subset of networks in the world are social networks. The key difference between social networks and other networks is that social networks have to involve people (or groups of people) and their perceptions, thoughts, interactions, and behaviors.
Sometimes interactions between people are mediated by technologies. For instance, people can connect with one another by texting on their phones or by traveling by plane, in which case the distinction between a technological and a social network becomes a matter of degree.
In this class, we will deal with networks that are closer to the “purely social” end of the scale: Those involving people, their perceptions, interactions, sentiments, exchanges, memberships, and relations. The primary perspective that we will take is that of social network analysis as developed in the discipline of sociology since the 1970s.








Figure 1: Social Science Disciplines that Contribute to and Use Social Network Analysis.




As noted, the interdisciplinary field that studies social networks is called social network analysis (SNA) and draws on insights from a variety of other social science disciplines, such as sociology, anthropology, psychology, and communication (see Figure 1). SNA, in turn, is part of an even larger interdisciplinary field, called network science, that studies all types of networks and includes work in physics, computer science, data science, biology, engineering, mathematics, and other fields. The relationships among these scientific fields are depicted in Figure 2.








Figure 2: The Network of Network Science.







Social network analysis has two broad aspects. One, generally referred to as network theory, is about understanding how networks work and what they do to and for people. In essence, social network theories are general statements about how people behave in networks and how networks themselves “behave”; that is where network relations come from, what they do, and what consequences they have for the people involved.
For instance, the idea of social capital, that is, the connections that you have to others, can bring you certain types of benefits, and is part of network theory. In fact, as we will see later, a good chunk of network theory (but not all of it), such as the theory of structural holes or the strength of weak ties theory, can be thought of as theories of social capital (Borgatti and Halgin 2011). Other types of network theory deal with how networks of sentiment relations (e.g., likes and dislikes) form, while others describe how things flow through networks.








Figure 3: The two faces of social network analysis.




Another branch of social network analysis deals with how to measure various network properties. This branch of social network analysis, called network measurement, links social network concepts to a mathematical or quantitative representation. Since this branch of network analysis deals with measurement, it is where mathematics and other quantitative representations of networks (such as matrices) come in handy.
If math scares you, don’t worry. Our job is to walk you through it slowly. But you still may be asking: Why math, though? The beauty of math is that it allows us to take some fuzzy social science concepts, stated in natural language, such as the ideas of “popularity,” “social position,” or “strength of connection,” and give them a precise representation. That way, we can use networks to learn what makes the social world go round or to predict why some people, organizations, or even whole countries are successful, and others are not (among other things).








Figure 4: Levels of analysis in social networks.




The two “faces” of SNA (network theory and network measurement), as well as some choice examples, are depicted in Figure 3. Don’t get nervous if you do not know what the things at the bottom of the diagram (e.g., “density”) mean. We will explain them to you in the forthcoming lessons.
We can develop theories or measure network properties at multiple levels of analysis. Like other complex systems, social networks feature dynamics at multiple nested levels. We will deal with five such levels in what follows.

At the node level, we may be interested in what properties nodes have by virtue of the connections they have within the network. Both the idea of an ego network and various measures of social position based on centrality are defined at this level.
At the dyad and triad levels, we may be interested in the properties that the edges or the links have by virtue of settling into certain configurations. Both the idea of tie strength and various theories dealing with triples of nodes, such as Balance Theory (Davis 1963), Strength of Weak Ties Theory (Granovetter 1973), the theory of Structural Holes (Burt 1995), and Simmelian Tie Theory (Krackhardt 1999) are defined at this level.
At the level of motifs may be interested in the network substructures or the “lego building blocks” that make up the larger network. For instance, how many configurations of three, four, or five actors can we observe?
At the subgroup or community level, we may be interested in properties that subsets, clusters, or nodes have by virtue of the set of connections they share. Here, theories and measures of group cohesion and community structure in networks have been developed.
Finally, we may be interested in measuring properties and theorizing the structure and dynamics of the whole network. This may include quantities that are sums or averages of features computed at lower levels, or properties applicable to the system as a whole (e.g., whether it would take a short or long time to get something from one randomly selected person in the network to another). Ideas of whether human networks constitute Small Worlds (Milgram 1967) are defined at this level.

In Figure 4, we can see how the nested structure of social networks can be depicted. At all levels, we can develop specific theories to understand what is happening in that slice, or develop special measures to link the concepts of those theories to a precise quantitative representation.



’Social network analysis is an influential, and now increasingly widespread, methodological approach for analyzing the social world. Traditionally, sociologists have studied relationships using a variety of observational strategies, both qualitative, such as ethnography and interviews, and quantitative, such as social surveys. However, beginning in earnest in the 1950s, sociologists began to make concerted use of mathematical techniques from a branch of pure mathematics called graph theory and a branch of applied mathematics called matrix algebra to develop scientific models of social relationships and to come up with measures connecting key concepts from social theory, such as roles, prominence, and prestige, to tangible empirical evidence.
Social Network Analysis (SNA) is the use of graph-theoretic and matrix-algebraic techniques to study social structure and social relationships in real-world networks. title: What is A Social Network?
text:
What are social networks? As you saw in the tree chart shown in ?@fig-network-types in the previous lesson, only a subset of networks in the world are social networks. The key difference between social networks and other networks is that social networks have to involve people (or groups of people) and their perceptions, thoughts, interactions, and behaviors.
Sometimes interactions between people are mediated by technologies. For instance, people can connect with one another by texting on their phones or by traveling by plane, in which case the distinction between a technological and a social network becomes a matter of degree.
In this class, we will deal with networks that are closer to the “purely social” end of the scale: Those involving people, their perceptions, interactions, sentiments, exchanges, memberships, and relations. The primary perspective that we will take is that of social network analysis as developed in the discipline of sociology since the 1970s.








Figure 1: Social Science Disciplines that Contribute to and Use Social Network Analysis.




As noted, the interdisciplinary field that studies social networks is called social network analysis (SNA) and draws on insights from a variety of other social science disciplines, such as sociology, anthropology, psychology, and communication (see Figure 1). SNA, in turn, is part of an even larger interdisciplinary field, called network science, that studies all types of networks and includes work in physics, computer science, data science, biology, engineering, mathematics, and other fields. The relationships among these scientific fields are depicted in Figure 2.








Figure 2: The Network of Network Science.

title: What is A Social Network?
text:
Social network analysis has two broad aspects. One, generally referred to as network theory, is about understanding how networks work and what they do to and for people. In essence, social network theories are general statements about how people behave in networks and how networks themselves “behave”; that is where network relations come from, what they do, and what consequences they have for the people involved.
For instance, the idea of social capital, that is, the connections that you have to others, can bring you certain types of benefits, and is part of network theory. In fact, as we will see later, a good chunk of network theory (but not all of it), such as the theory of structural holes or the strength of weak ties theory, can be thought of as theories of social capital (Borgatti and Halgin 2011). Other types of network theory deal with how networks of sentiment relations (e.g., likes and dislikes) form, while others describe how things flow through networks.








Figure 3: The two faces of social network analysis.




Another branch of social network analysis deals with how to measure various network properties. This branch of social network analysis, called network measurement, links social network concepts to a mathematical or quantitative representation. Since this branch of network analysis deals with measurement, it is where mathematics and other quantitative representations of networks (such as matrices) come in handy.
If math scares you, don’t worry. Our job is to walk you through it slowly. But you still may be asking: Why math, though? The beauty of math is that it allows us to take some fuzzy social science concepts, stated in natural language, such as the ideas of “popularity,” “social position,” or “strength of connection,” and give them a precise representation. That way, we can use networks to learn what makes the social world go round or to predict why some people, organizations, or even whole countries are successful, and others are not (among other things).








Figure 4: Levels of analysis in social networks.




The two “faces” of SNA (network theory and network measurement), as well as some choice examples, are depicted in Figure 3. Don’t get nervous if you do not know what the things at the bottom of the diagram (e.g., “density”) mean. We will explain them to you in the forthcoming lessons.
We can develop theories or measure network properties at multiple levels of analysis. Like other complex systems, social networks feature dynamics at multiple nested levels. We will deal with five such levels in what follows.

At the node level, we may be interested in what properties nodes have by virtue of the connections they have within the network. Both the idea of an ego network and various measures of social position based on centrality are defined at this level.
At the dyad and triad levels, we may be interested in the properties that the edges or the links have by virtue of settling into certain configurations. Both the idea of tie strength and various theories dealing with triples of nodes, such as Balance Theory (Davis 1963), Strength of Weak Ties Theory (Granovetter 1973), the theory of Structural Holes (Burt 1995), and Simmelian Tie Theory (Krackhardt 1999) are defined at this level.
At the level of motifs may be interested in the network substructures or the “lego building blocks” that make up the larger network. For instance, how many configurations of three, four, or five actors can we observe?
At the subgroup or community level, we may be interested in properties that subsets, clusters, or nodes have by virtue of the set of connections they share. Here, theories and measures of group cohesion and community structure in networks have been developed.
Finally, we may be interested in measuring properties and theorizing the structure and dynamics of the whole network. This may include quantities that are sums or averages of features computed at lower levels, or properties applicable to the system as a whole (e.g., whether it would take a short or long time to get something from one randomly selected person in the network to another). Ideas of whether human networks constitute Small Worlds (Milgram 1967) are defined at this level.

In Figure 4, we can see how the nested structure of social networks can be depicted. At all levels, we can develop specific theories to understand what is happening in that slice, or develop special measures to link the concepts of those theories to a precise quantitative representation.

title: Theories of Valenced Interactions
text:
In the study of social networks, understanding how positive and negative relationships manifest and influence network structure is crucial. These relationships are often referred to as valenced interactions or valenced ties. The idea of valence in a tie refers to a tie property, mainly that a particular link can be either positive or negative.
As we saw in ?@sec-sbalance, a network incorporating these positive and negative sentiments can be represented using a signed graph featuring distinct sets of positive and negative links. For instance, “liking,” “hating,” “admiring,” “loving,” “bullying,” and “fighting” are examples of interpersonal sentiments and interactions that represent valenced ties within an ego network. Liking, admiring, and loving are examples of ties with positive valence, while hating, bullying, and fighting are examples of ties with negative valence. Network analysts have developed several specific theories aiming to explain how individuals form and manage these valenced interactions in social networks.
Karma Theory, Status Theory, and Solidarity Theory are social psychological theories that aim to explain expected patterns of relationships within sentiment networks. These theories build upon the broader concept of Balance Theory, which was first described by Fritz Heider (1946) and posits that people are motivated to seek balance in their triadic social configurations (see ?@sec-tbalance). They predict how an individual might form sentiments towards another person based on the existing sentiment relations between that alter and other members of the network.


Karma Theory’s central idea is “You get what you spread out!”. It proposes that individuals tend to reciprocate the feelings or sentiments that someone sends out towards others. If an individual exhibits negative behavior or rudeness without clear provocation, others are likely to respond with negativity towards them. Conversely, if someone is kind and positive towards others, they are likely to receive positive sentiments in return. This theory specifically predicts valenced “indegree” (the sentiments one receives) based on valenced “outdegree” (the sentiments one sends out). The common expressions “bullies get bullied” and “likers get liked” illustrate this principle, indicating that the sentiments an individual expresses towards others tend to be returned to them.








Figure 1: Illustration of Karma Theory (You get what you receive).





Examples:

If S is described as a rude person, Karma Theory predicts that you would feel negatively towards him, as their outward negative valences are reciprocated.
If M is a friendly person who is consistently nice to everyone, Karma Theory predicts that you would like him, mirroring the positive valences he sends out.




Status Theory suggests that people’s sentiments towards an alter are heavily influenced by how others in the network feel towards that same alter. It can be considered an extension of the triadic balance theory we discussed in ?@sec-tbalance.
A fundamental principle of status theory is that individuals tend to mimic or align their sentiments with those that others send towards a potential alter. If someone is liked by many in the network, you are more likely to like them too. This alignment can stem from a psychological desire for balance, to avoid conflict with existing relationships, or from the assumption that others might possess more information about the alter. Accordingly, a node’s status in valenced networks is determined by the sign of the ties it receives, according to the following principles:

High status is associated with receiving many incoming positive ties.
Low status is associated with receiving many incoming negative ties.
A directed positive tie from ego to alter suggests that ego considers alter to have higher status.
A directed negative tie from ego to alter suggests that ego considers alter to have lower status.

In the same way, the sign of the directed ties you send to others impacts your own status, according to the following principles:

Positive ties to high-status individuals increase one’s status.
Positive ties to low-status individuals decrease one’s status.
Negative ties to high-status individuals decrease one’s status.
Negative ties to low-status individuals increase one’s status.

Status theory posits that individuals generally strive to avoid losing status and actively seek ways to boost it. This leads to the following observable patterns:

High-status individuals tend to accumulate positive ties, illustrating a “rich get richer” effect.
Low-status individuals may accumulate negative ties, described as a “gang up” effect.
Over time, high-status individuals tend to lose negative ties, while low-status individuals tend to lose positive ties.

Examples:

If everyone likes Aruna (and thus Aruna is a high status actor in the network), Status Theory predicts that you would also like Aruna, as you would align your sentiment with the positive valences she receives from others, while boosting your own status.
If B is not liked by anyone (and thus B is a low status actor in the network), Status Theory predicts that you would also decide not to like B, aligning your sentiment with the existing negative sentiment in the network, thus also boosting your own status.
If C enters a new setting and forms a positive bond with M who is disliked by many others (and is thus low status), C is predicted to withdraw the positive tie to M.
If W enters a new setting and forms a negative impression of X who is liked by many others (and is thus highg status), W is predicted to over time become more positive toward X.




Solidarity Theory posits that individuals feel positively towards others who are similarly socially situated within a sentiment network, and negatively towards those who are differently situated. This theory highlights that shared social positions or mutual recognition of one’s place in the network can be a strong motivator for positive ties. In the theory shared position is measured according to status, such that individuals who receive lots of positive ties from others are in the same (high status) position, as are individuals who receive lots of negative ties from others, who occupy a similar (low status) position.









Examples:

If you and another person (D) are both generally disliked in the overall network, your shared negative position can create an incentive for you to like one another, contrasting with the dislike you receive from others. This is described as the “downtrodden stick together!” effect.
Conversely, if two people are both liked within the network, they share a similar high status position. This shared similarity provides an incentive for them to like one another, representing a “popular in-crowd” or “cool kids stick together!” effect.
If one person is liked by many others but another is heavily disliked, they do not share a similar social position. In such cases, Solidarity Theory predicts that the sentiment between these two differentially situated individuals will be negative. For example, if “No one likes Christophe,” your sentiment towards him will depend on your own social position. If you are also disliked, you might like Christophe; but if you are liked, you would not like Christophe because you don’t share the same social position.

title: Social Ties and Network Boundaries
text:
This is likely not your first sociology course. But even if it is, relationships are relatively intuitive for people. They are all around us: you and your parents, you and your siblings, your siblings and your parents, you and your classmates, your classmates to each other. Affiliation, communication, friendship, hatred: these are the content of social relationships. Two people either have a relationship of some kind or they do not.
Essentially, a relationship is a connection between at least two social actors. We will see that sometimes, when relations clump together into networks, two sets of relations can have different content, but still share the same form (e.g., arrangement, or pattern).
The technical social networks term for “relations clumping together into networks” is concatenation (Martin 2009). For instance, every time you introduce two previously unrelated acquaintances to one another, you concatenate two previous disconnected ties into a connected triple called a triad.


For example, you are likely enrolled in a social network’s class if you are reading this, and have people you know, such as your friends and people you’ve taken prior classes with, but also people you’ve never seen before. It might be obvious that you have a relationship with those people that you know, but do you have a relationship with those you do not know?






Figure 1: “One of the first pictures of a social network, then called a ‘sociogram’ was drawn by Jacob Moreno in 1934. It consisted of the relationships between 19 boys (triangles) and 18 girls (circles) in a 5th grade classroom”



The answer is maybe. It depends on how you define the term social relationship. If you were asked who your friends are, you would tell me that some of your classmates are your friends, and the rest are not. If you were asked which of these people in your classroom are your classmates, everyone would be your classmate, except for your professor or teaching assistants. You share a particular type of equivalence relationship with these other people, your classmates, even if you’ve never met them. The word “classmate” even implies a relationship type, one with a different social meaning than “friend.” When analyzing a social network, it is important to first understand the type of social relationship you are examining, as this directly affects the conclusions or generalizations you can draw about the social world.



Once you have a type of social relationship you would like to examine, the next step is to bound the context. If you want to map out all the social relationships in the world, well, that’s impossible. Imagine how difficult it would be to map out all the people at your school who are friends with one another. That might be feasible if you have only 1,000 undergraduates, but at a school of 30,000, it would be a nightmare. That is in part why it is so important to bound the social context. The other is to exclude relationships that are not meaningful for your study. Bounding, or to draw boundaries, is to have a rule about what will or will not be included in the study (Laumann et al. 1989).






Figure 2: “The Zachary karate club network study was one of the first data collection projects in the history of SNA. The data are famous for showing how networks could be used to find groups based on the relations between actors.”



For example, if you are interested in who is friends with whom in your social networks class, you have bound your study to look at only people who are in your social networks class. One of the most famous social network studies was performed by the anthropologist Wayne W. Zachary (see Figure 2) at a college karate club in the 1970s (Zachary 1977). Thus, the 34 members of the karate club and the outside teacher were the actors included in the study because they were involved in the day-to-day operations of the karate club at the time the data were collected.
With a type of social relationship in some bounded context, you can begin to map the social world as a graph. In its most basic form, a graph is essentially a picture of the relationships between different types of social actors. This picture becomes incredibly powerful when we use mathematical concepts to understand how actors relate to one another (which this book is mostly concerned with) or to identify the social principles on which the network may have been formed.
While this class will mostly use the terms node and edge when referring to graphs, these are not the only terms in use among those who use network analysis techniques. Additional names for nodes include vertex or point. Relationships between two nodes are, in addition to being called edges, referred to as ties or links.
